list.listitem: Electrophysiologic (EP) studies are recommended for symptomatic patients in whom sinus node dysfunction (SND) is suspected but for whom a causal relationship has not been established. C
Permanent pacemaker is recommended in patients with sinus node dysfunction with documented symptomatic bradycardia. C
Permanent dual chamber pacing has no survival benefit but does relieve symptoms and reduce syncopal attacks. B
Other possible indications include symptomatic chronotropic incompetence, bradycardia due to medications that cannot be discontinued, and syncope associated with major abnormalities on EPS studies. C

background.definition: Sinus node dysfunction (SND or sick sinus syndrome) constitutes a spectrum of cardiac arrhythmias, including sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, sinoatrial block, and paroxysmal supraventricular tachyarrhythmias alternating with periods of bradycardia or even asystole.

list.listitem: The incidence in general population increases with age; sinus node dysfunction (SND) occurs in approximately 2 per 1000 persons older than 65 years.
The incidence of SND after cardiac transplantation is 175 persons per 1000 patients.
After acute myocardial infarction, the incidence of SND is 46 per 1000 patients.
The mortality associated wth SND has been estimated at 4 to 5% annually with embolic events accounting for 30-50% of those deaths.
Idiopathic degeneration.
Ischemia including myocardial infarction and chronic nodal artery ischemia .
Inflammatory diseases like rheumatic fever, Chagas disease, Lyme disease, and other infections.
Epicardial, myocardial and pericardial diseases.
Infiltrative disorders like amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, and tumors.
Collagen vascular diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and scleroderma.
Medications such as beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, lithium and antiarrhythmics.
Congenital.
Trauma during cardiac surgery.
Heart transplantation.
Augmented vagal tone in athletes.
Metabolic abnormalities like hypothyroidism, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and hypoxia.

Sinus node dysfunction (SND) is caused by either intrinsic or extrinsic etiologies, or both. Intrinsic sinus node function deteriorates with age due to increasing degree of fibrosis, amyloid deposition and atrophy. Extrinsic etiologies such as high vagal tone and drugs are seen more commonly in younger patients.
Invasion of the area near the sinus node with tumor cells and inflammatory cells may compromise the physiologic function.
Sinoatrial block results in delay or even nonconduction of impulses through the sinoatrial node to the atrium. The atrioventricular node is also affected in as many as 65% of patients.
SND may be transient due to medications and completely reversible once the offending medications are withdrawn.
Bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome (BTS) is characterized by both bradycardia which is due to SND and supraventricular tachycardias which are probably due to diffuse disease of the conduction system.
Routine 12 lead ECG is the recommended initial diagnostic test. Ambulatory ECG (Holter) monitoring may aid in the diagnosis. C
Electrophysiologic (EP) studies are recommended for symptomatic patients in whom sinus node dysfunction (SND) is suspected as the cause but for whom a causal relation has not been established. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Atrial impulses (P waves) waves seen with delay or nonconduction to ventricle
Fibrillatory waves, irregularly irregular QRS complexes
Orthostatic hypotension, related to emotional situation, pain, coughing and micturition

list.listitem: Sinus arrhythmia: normal P wave morphology and axis; gradual phasic change in PP interval of more than 10% or 120 ms is seen in response to breathing.
Sinus bradycardia: sinus rate less than 60 beats/minute with normal P wave axis.
Sinoatrial exit block Mobitz I: normal P wave morphology/axis and pauses with no visible sinus P waves; progressive increase in the PR interval occurs before the pause.
Sinoatrial exit block Mobitz II: normal P wave morphology/axis; pauses with no visible sinus P waves. Constant PP interval before and after pause.
Sinus arrest/pause: a pause without a P wave more than 2.0 seconds during sinus rhythm.
Ascertained sick sinus syndrome: good correlation between symptoms and bradycardia.

Possible sick sinus syndrome: uncertain cause and effect relationship between symptoms and bradycardia in patients with signs of severe sinus dysfunction after other possible causes have been excluded.

Patients with bradycardic episodes may present with symptoms resulting from cardiac and cerebral hypoperfusion, such as angina, shortness of breath, exercise intolerance, fatigue, syncope, presyncope, and dizziness.
Patients with episodes of bradyarrhythmias and tachyarrhythmias may present with palpitations, shortness of breath, angina, and sometimes flash pulmonary edema.
Paroxysmal episodes of atrial fibrillation in patients may result in stroke or systemic embolism.
Patients may also exhibit clinical manifestations of the underlying etiology.
Physical examination is of limited value apart from detecting abnormally slow or irregularly fast pulse.

Routine 12 lead ECG is the recommended initial diagnostic test to detect sinus node dysfunction (SND). For patients with paroxysmal symptoms or episodes, continuous monitoring with 24 to 48 hours holter monitor, 30 day event monitor or 18 to 24 months implantable loop recorder may be helpful. Symptoms not correlating well with the rhythm disturbances recorded on ECG are of little significance.

Abnormal autonomic reflexes play an important role in causing the clinical symptoms of SSS patients and can help in evaluating nodal dysfunction via carotid sinus massage, tilt table testing, and valsalva maneuver.

Carotid sinus massage is one of the diagnostic maneuvers used in patients older than 40 years with syncope. After carotid massage, more than 3 seconds of asystole or sinus pause is considered positive. There is a risk of stroke associated with this maneuver if carotid disease is present.
Valsalva maneuver will not increase the heart rate in patients with SND in comparison to individuals with normal sinus node function.
Pharmacologic evaluation with atropine or isoproterenol can also be used for diagnosing SND. Increase in the heart rate less than 25% or below 90 beats/minute is considered abnormal.
Marked chronotropic incompetence is associated with SND but its role in diagnosing nodal dysfunction is limited due to its low sensitivity and specificity.

EP study is recommended in symptomatic patients in whom SND is suspected, but in whom a causal relation has not been established. Sinoatrial node recovery time (SNRT) and sinoatrial conduction time (SACT) are the most frequently performed tests.

SNRT is most useful for analyzing SN automaticity. Pacing is interrupted after 30 seconds or longer of overdrive atrial pacing and the escape interval or SNRT is measured. SNRT of more than 1600 ms is abnormal. This is often corrected for underlying baseline sinus cycle length and is called the corrected sinus node recovery time (CSNRT). CSNRT more than 450 ms is considered abnormal.
In many patients the delay in conduction of impulse from sinus node to atrium is the main abnormality and is measured as the SACT. Unidirectional SACT more than 120 ms is considered abnormal.
SND is typically diagnosed incidentally on an ECG or in patients presenting with a variety of cardiovascular symptoms.
Diagnosis is confirmed by ECG or by ambulatory ECG (Holter) monitoring.
Order EP studies for symptomatic patients when SND is suspected but a causal relation cannot be established.
See algorithm in for an overview of treatment.
Permanent pacemaker is recommended in SND patients with documented symptomatic bradycardia. C

Permanent pacemaker is also recommended in patients with bradycardia as a result of essential long-term drug therapy for which there are no acceptable alternatives and for symptomatic chronotropic incompetence. C

Syncope of unexplained origin when major abnormalities of sinus node function are discovered or provoked on EPS, and SND with heart rate less than 40 bpm and unclear relationship between symptoms and bradycardia, are also possible indications for permanent pacing although the evidence is conflicting. C

See algorithm in for an overview of treatment. Asymptomatic SND patients do not require treatment and can be observed. Antiarrhythmic drugs in combination with pacemaker may be used to control tachyarrhythmias in bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome (BTS).

In patients paced for SND who have atrial tachyarrhythmias, class IC antiarrhythmics (propafenone, flecainide, and sotalol) are not inferior to amiodarone in terms of the combined endpoints of death, permanent atrial tachycardia, hospitalizations, cardioversions and antiarrhythmic change.
Anticoagulation is required in patients with atrial fibrillation with an elevated risk of embolic stroke if they have a low bleeding risk.
See for pacemaker indications.

In patients with SND, dual chamber pacemaker reduces the risk of atrial fibrillation (ARR 3.9%, NNT 26), reduces signs and symptoms of heart failure and slightly improves quality of life as compared with ventricular pacing. There is no difference in the risk of stroke between dual chamber and ventricular pacing, based on 5664 patient years of follow-up in one study (2.2% at 1 year, 5.8% at 4 years).
Cardiac pacing can reduce falls in patients with sick sinus syndrome.
In some patients with BTS, radiofrequency ablation to prevent recurrence of atrial fibrillation may resolve symptoms.
Temporary pacing may be used in symptomatic patients awaiting permanent pacemaker placement.
Treat reversible causes such as hypothermia, hypothyroidism, and hypoglycemia.
Correct electrolyte abnormalities such as hyperkalemia.
Treat infections such as Lyme disease, rheumatic fever.
Stop calcium channel blockers, beta blockers and digoxin until and unless they arerequired and no alternatives are available.
Hospitalize patients with symptomatic bradycardia in SND as well as to address reversible causes such as hypothermia and hypoglycemia.
Refer patients to cardiologists or electrophysiologists to determine the need for EP study and pacemaker placement. All patients with symptomatic SSS should also be referred to a cardiologist.
Thromboembolism: anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3) or direct oral anticoagulants per atrial fibrillation management guidelines.
Atrial fibrillation: anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3) or direct oral anticoagulants.
Syncope: pacemaker implantation.
Arrhythmia: antiarrhythmics, anticoagulation, pacemaker and maybe radiofrequency ablation.
Congestive heart failure: diuretics, pacemaker implantation.
Permanent dual chamber pacing has no survival benefit but does relieve symptoms and reduce syncopal attacks. B
Schedule follow-up for patients with SSS, depending on the type of pacemaker implanted and their management needs. C

Sinus bradycardia as the sole manifestation of cardiac disease in the elderly patient has little effect on mortality. The overall 5-year survival rate of nonpaced sinus bradycardia patients is 74.8%, not significantly different from the 72% rate in the general population with similar age and sex distribution.
SND progresses slowly and usually takes 7 to 29 years (average 13 years) for total sinus arrest to manifest.

Clinical cardiovascular events such as syncope, heart failure, chronic atrial fibrillation and poorly tolerated paroxysmal tachyarrhythmias develop in majority (57%) of untreated SND patients during long term follow-up.
Mortality does not seem to be affected by permanent pacing in SND.
Atrial or dual chamber pacing is associated with lower incidence of heart failure, fewer episodes of syncope, lower risk of atrial fibrillation and overall better quality of life.
Syncope in subjects who undergo pacing for SND can occur in up to 20% of patients (over a 5 year follow up period).
Pacemaker function should be assessed before discharge from hospital.
Periodic transtelephonic monitoring with intermittent clinic evaluation to assess pacemaker function.
Clinical follow-up should occur twice in the first 6 months and then once every 12 months for single chamber pacemaker patients.
Dual chamber pacemaker patients should follow up twice in the first 6 months and then once every 6 months.
Clinic follow-up includes assessment of the clinical status, battery status, pacing threshold and pulse width, sensing function, lead integrity, and optimization of sensor driven rate response.
Avoid calcium channel blockers, beta blockers, digoxin and antiarrhythmics (may further suppress a sick SA node or unmask latent SND) until and unless there are no alternatives available.
Avoid contact sports.
Avoid strong magnetic fields if pacemakers are implanted.
In case of any symptoms follow with clinic immediately.
Dual chamber pacemaker implantation improves quality of life in elderly patients with SND.

Significant SND occurs most frequently in children with congenital heart disease such as atrial septal defect (particularly following corrective heart surgery), in acquired myocardial disease, with certain medications, and in children with high vagal tone.

Permanent pacing is recommended in children, adolescents and patients with congenital heart disease presenting with following conditions: (1) SND with correlation of symptoms during age inappropriate bradycardia; (2) brady tachy syndrome requiring long term antiarrhythmic treatment; and (3) asymptomatic sinus bradycardia in children with complex congenital heart disease with resting heart rate less than 40 bpm or pauses in ventricular rate of more than 3 seconds.

feature.caption: ACC/AHA Indications of Permanent Pacing in Sinus Node Dysfunction.
feature.feature_body:
Conditions for which there is evidence and/or general agreement that permanent pacing is useful and effective
Sinus node dysfunction patients with documented symptomatic bradycardia Patients with bradycardia as a result of essential long-term drug therapy for which there are no acceptable alternatives Symptomatic chronotropic incompetence
Conditions for which there is conflicting evidence, but the weight of evidence is in favor of usefulness and efficacy
Sinus node dysfunction occurring spontaneously or as a result of necessary drug therapy (HR <40 bpm) when a clear association between significant symptoms and bradycardia has not been documented Syncope of unknown origin when major abnormalities of sinus node function are discovered or provoked in electrophysiologic studies
